You can process the data in the AWS cloud (or download directly) using the URL schemes s3://commoncrawl/[...], https://ds5q9oxwqwsfj.cloudfront.net/[...] and https://data.commoncrawl.org/[...].  

To access data from outside the Amazon cloud, via HTTP(S), the new URL prefix https://data.commoncrawl.org/ – must be used.  

For further detail on the data file formats listed below, please visit the [ISO Website](https://iso.org/), which provides format standards, information and documentation. There are also helpful explanations and details regarding file formats in other GitHub projects.  

The status of our infrastructure can be monitored on our [**Infra Status**](https://status.commoncrawl.org) page.  

Accessing the data in the AWS Cloud

It’s mandatory to access the data from the region where it is located (us-east-1 ).  

The connection to S3 should be faster and you avoid the minimal fees for inter-region data transfer (you have to send requests which are charged as outgoing traffic).  

Be careful using an Elastic IP address or load balancer, because you may be charged for the routed traffic.

You may use the [AWS Command Line Interface](https://aws.amazon.com/cli/) but many AWS services (e.g EMR) support the s3:// protocol, and you may directly specify your input as s3://commoncrawl/path_to_file, sometimes even using wildcards.  

On Hadoop (not EMR) it’s recommended to use the [S3A Protocol](https://stackoverflow.com/questions/33356041/technically-what-is-the-difference-between-s3n-s3a-and-s3): just change the protocol to s3a://.

Accessing the data from outside the AWS Cloud

If you want to download the data to your local machine or local cluster, you can use any HTTP download agent, such as [cURL](https://github.com/curl/curl) or [wget](https://www.gnu.org/software/wget/). The data is accessible via the https://data.commoncrawl.org/[...] URL scheme.  

There is no need to create an AWS account in order to access the data using this method.

Using the AWS Command Line Interface

The [AWS Command Line Interface](https://aws.amazon.com/cli/) can be used to access the data from anywhere (including EC2). It’s easy to install on most operating systems (Windows, macOS, Linux). Please follow the [installation instructions](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/cli/latest/userguide/getting-started-install.html).  

Please note, access to data from the Amazon cloud using the S3 API is only allowed for authenticated users. Please see our [blog announcement](https://commoncrawl.org/blog/introducing-cloudfront-access-to-common-crawl-data) for more information.  

Once the AWS CLI is installed, the command to copy a file to your local machine is:  
aws s3 cp s3://commoncrawl/path_to_file <local_path>‍  
You may first look at the data e.g, to list all WARC files of a specific segment of the April 2018 crawl:  
> aws s3 ls s3://commoncrawl/crawl-data/CC-MAIN-2018-17/segments/1524125937193.1/warc/

aws s3 cp help

To download a file using an HTTP download agent add the full path to the prefix https://data.commoncrawl.org/, e.g:

import json
import re
from urllib.parse import urlencode
from urllib.request import urlopen

endpoint = 'https://datasets-server.huggingface.co/rows'
query = urlencode({
    'dataset': 'ai4bharat/sangraha',
    'config': 'synthetic',
    'split': 'hin_Deva',
    'offset': 2552319,
    'length': 100,
})
with urlopen(f'{endpoint}?{query}', timeout=30) as response:
    rows = json.load(response)['rows']
tag_names = []
for entry in rows:
    tag_names.extend(
        match.group(1).lower()
        for match in re.finditer(r'(?is)</?\s*([a-z][a-z0-9:-]*)\b[^>]{0,390}>', entry['row'].get('text', ''))
    )
print({
    'unique_tag_names': sorted(set(tag_names)),
    'html_document_markers': sorted(set(tag_names) & {'html', 'head', 'body', 'doctype'}),
    'tag_occurrences': len(tag_names),
})

| `synthetic/hin_Deva` | 2,552,319 | `doc_id`, `text` | no HTML document |

The dataset metadata exposes only three configurations: `verified`, `unverified`, and `synthetic`.

**Conclusion:** no Sangraha subset exposes an `html`, `url`, WARC-path, PDF-byte, image, or source-layout field. The `synthetic/hin_Deva` window produced six broad angle-bracket-regex hits, but strict classification found only one `<unk>` token and **no** `html`, `head`, `body`, or `doctype` markers. That is residual model/text markup, not a retained HTML document.

## Datasets/sources that do retain markup

### Recommended if actual HTML extraction is the objective: Common Crawl WARC

Use **Common Crawl WARC**, specifically—not WET.

- **WARC**: captured HTTP responses, including original HTML. Suitable for Trafilatura, jusText, Readability, Inscriptis, Resiliparse, extruct, and DOM/model-based extractors.
- **WET**: already-extracted text. It would recreate the same limitation as Sangraha.
- **Index records**: enable selective retrieval by URL/domain and HTTP metadata before fetching WARC byte ranges.

For a Hindi case study, a defensible path is:

```text
Common Crawl WARC
  → select likely Indian/Hindi web domains or broad HTML responses
  → fetch original HTML records
  → language-identify text after conservative extraction
  → stop once the retained Hindi sample reaches 10–100M tokens
```

This would make the extraction stage substantive, but increases acquisition, provenance, copyright, and language-validation work.

Source: [Common Crawl — Get Started](https://commoncrawl.org/get-started). It documents public crawl access and explicitly lists downloadable `.warc.gz` files.

### Good markup-cleaning alternative, but not raw HTML: Hindi Wikipedia XML

The official [Hindi Wikipedia pages-articles XML dump](https://dumps.wikimedia.org/hiwiki/latest/) is currently available as a ~248 MB multistream compressed XML dump.

It retains **MediaWiki wikitext/templates/references/categories**, so it supports real markup extraction and structural cleanup. It does **not** retain the original website HTML/DOM.

This is easier to reproduce and license-track than Common Crawl, but is less representative of noisy web extraction. It also changes the project’s data regime from open web to encyclopedic text.

- **Use Hindi Wikipedia XML** if the desired extraction demonstration is template/wikitext cleanup rather than web-DOM extraction.

| **[Common Crawl WARC](https://commoncrawl.org/get-started)** | Raw HTTP responses, including original HTML; WARC path/offset metadata through the crawl index | **Best authentic web-extraction source.** Filter HTML responses, retrieve the source bytes, apply language ID after extraction, and stop at 10–100M retained tokens. | More engineering: index queries, byte-range WARC retrieval, deduplication, provenance, and copyright/terms handling. |

This is the closest clean substitution if the goal is to demonstrate extraction techniques rather than merely residual cleanup.

```text
html
url
text
html_head
html_title
html_footer
metadata_html
c4_shard
c4_timestamp
HtmlPreprocessor_error
```

```text
raw HTML
  → Trafilatura / jusText / Readability / Inscriptis
  → compare extracted main content
  → compare with supplied text/title/head/footer metadata
  → measure retained chars/tokens, boilerplate removal,
    extractor disagreement, language, duplicates, PII, and provenance
```

A focused Hugging Face API search for **“hindi html”** returned no ready-made dataset. Sangraha’s other configurations also do not retain source HTML.

```text
Common Crawl WARC
  → select candidate HTML records
  → extract text conservatively
  → identify Hindi after extraction
  → retain a 10–100M-token Hindi subset
```

---
name: marimo-pair
description: >-
  Drive a live marimo notebook as a workspace: run Python in the same kernel
  the user does, inspect live notebook state, and commit durable notebook
  changes. Use when the user wants to start a marimo notebook or pair on an
  active marimo session.
allowed-tools: Bash(bash **/scripts/discover-servers.sh *), Bash(bash **/scripts/execute-code.sh *), Read
---

marimo is a reactive Python runtime for building reproducible Python programs
(marimo notebooks). Cells are connected by the variables they define and
reference. Running a cell re-executes dependents in dataflow order. The active
runtime holds the kernel namespace, cell state, and dataflow graph. The
notebook (`.py` file) is the artifact the kernel writes from that state while a
session is running.

A user interacts with the same runtime via a notebook UI with cells, outputs,
and widgets.

**WARNING. The active runtime is the source of truth.** During a session, you
SHOULD NOT modify the associated `.py` file directly. File edits WILL NOT reach
the active kernel or user, and the kernel may overwrite them on save. Use
`marimo._code_mode` (`cm`) for notebook changes. Reading disk is fine, but
prefer `ctx.cells[...].code` for current cell code.

## Connect to a Notebook

Use the bundled script (`bash scripts/execute-code.sh`) or MCP
(`execute_code(...)`) to run Python in a live marimo kernel.

If the user provides a notebook URL, target it directly:

```bash
bash scripts/execute-code.sh --url http://localhost:2718 -c "print('connected')"
```

Use `-c` only for short one-liners. For multiline code or code containing
quotes, backticks, `$`, or braces, use a single-quoted heredoc:

```bash
bash scripts/execute-code.sh --url http://localhost:2718 <<'PY'
import marimo._code_mode as cm

async with cm.get_context() as ctx:
    cid = ctx.create_cell("x = df.head()")
    ctx.run_cell(cid)
PY
```

When code already lives in a file, pass the file path:

```bash
bash scripts/execute-code.sh --url http://localhost:2718 /tmp/code.py
```

If no target is provided, find or start a session. First look for a running
session with `bash scripts/discover-servers.sh`, MCP `list_sessions()`, or
local process context. When multiple sessions are possible, target with
`--url`, `--port`, or `--session`.

If no server is running and the user wants a notebook, start marimo with
`--no-token` (and without `--headless`) so it auto-registers for discovery. The
notebook UI must be open before there is an active session for `execute-code`
to target. The right way to invoke marimo depends on context (project tooling,
global install, sandbox mode). If the notebook file contains a PEP 723 `#
/// script` header, it MUST be opened with `--sandbox` — otherwise marimo
ignores the inline dependencies. See
[finding-marimo.md](reference/finding-marimo.md) for the full decision tree and
[execution-context.md](reference/execution-context.md) for scripts, MCP, and
shell quoting.

## Scratchpad Scope

`execute-code` evaluates Python in marimo's scratchpad: a temporary namespace
with a shallow copy of the kernel globals. Notebook variables are available by
name, but new top-level bindings and rebindings are discarded after each call.
In-place mutations to notebook-owned objects can persist because those names
still reference live objects.

Each call reports stdout and stderr from the scratchpad, plus console output
from notebook cells it causes to run, including reactive descendants.

### Ordinary Python

Use ordinary Python in the scratchpad to inspect variables, sample data, test
transformations, probe APIs, check imports, and read widget state.

```python
print(df.head())

x = 10
print(x)
```

Here `df` comes from notebook globals, while `x` is a scratchpad-local binding.
`x` exists for this call only and WILL NOT be added to notebook globals.

### Persist with `cm`

Top-level scratchpad assignments and rebindings are temporary. To persist work,
including new variables, you MUST submit changes through `marimo._code_mode`
(`cm`).

`marimo._code_mode` is a PRIVATE, UNSTABLE agent API (note the leading
underscore). It exists for tools like this skill to drive a live kernel from
the scratchpad. DO NOT import it from notebook cells, library code, or
anything a user would run — methods can change or disappear across marimo
versions and kernels. Treat every `import marimo._code_mode as cm` as
scratchpad-only.

At session start, inspect what `cm` exposes in the active kernel:

```python
import marimo._code_mode as cm

help(cm)
```

Open a code-mode context to queue notebook changes.

```python
import marimo._code_mode as cm

async with cm.get_context() as ctx:
    cid = ctx.create_cell("x = df.head()")
    ctx.run_cell(cid)
```

The scratchpad supports top-level async code. Use `async with` directly;
wrapping it in `asyncio.run(...)` is unnecessary and can conflict with the
kernel's event loop.

After this block exits and the new cell runs, `x` is notebook state. Later
scratchpad calls can read `x` by name. Code later in the same scratchpad call
should read `ctx.globals["x"]`, because the scratchpad namespace was copied
before the cell ran.

Inside the context, queued mutation methods are synchronous. Call them
directly; do not `await` them. Each call queues an operation for marimo to
apply when the context exits normally. If the block raises, the queue is
discarded.

On clean exit, marimo applies packages, validates and applies structural cell
changes, runs queued cells, then may run dependents. Validation is only
structural since queued cell runs can still error. `create_cell` and
`edit_cell` change notebook structure only. Use `run_cell` to execute. 

`create_cell` currently defaults to `hide_code=True`, which collapses the code
editor in the UI. Pass `hide_code=False` if the user wants created cells to
be visible without manually expanding them.


## Marimo Rules

marimo imposes a small contract on notebook code so it can keep the notebook as
a directed acyclic graph (DAG):

- **No cycles** - cells cannot depend on each other in a cycle.
- **No public redefinitions across cells** - each name has one owning cell.
- **No wildcard imports** - `import *` prevents static analysis of definitions.

These rules keep the kernel, UI, and saved artifact consistent.

When `cm` submits a cell body, marimo parses its top-level definitions and
references. A top-level name enters the graph unless it is private with a
leading underscore.

```python
# Public definitions: values, total, i, value, mean
values = np.array([1, 2, 3])
total = 0
for i, value in enumerate(values):
    total += value
mean = total / len(values)
mean
```

```python
# Public definition: mean
_values = np.array([1, 2, 3])
_total = 0
for _i, _value in enumerate(_values):
    _total += _value
mean = _total / len(_values)
mean
```

Use private names for intermediates that no other cell should read. Public
names define the notebook-level dataflow. If a `cm` edit violates the contract,
marimo rejects the structural change and returns the validation error.

## The Notebook's Shape

A notebook is an ordered collection of cells. `ctx.cells` is the document view
and `ctx.graph` is the dataflow view.

```python
for cell in ctx.cells:
    cell  # .id, .code, .name, .config, .status, .errors

ctx.cells["setup"]         # by name
ctx.cells[0]               # by position
list(ctx.cells.keys())     # all IDs, in notebook order
```

Cell IDs are opaque strings which can be queried from the notebook or captured
from `cm` return values:

```python
cid = ctx.create_cell("df = pd.read_csv('data.csv')")
print(cid)   # e.g. 'Hbol'
```

Alternatively, cells can be assigned and referenced by `name`. The graph can be
used to understand its role in the dataflow.

```python
for cid, impl in ctx.graph.cells.items():
    impl  # .defs, .refs   (sets of public names)

ctx.graph.descendants(cid)   # cells that re-run when this one changes
ctx.graph.ancestors(cid)     # cells this one depends on
```

In marimo, deletes are *destructive* so it can be useful to query the
descendants prior to deleting to understand it's impact.

## Writing Notebook Changes

The graph contract keeps marimo able to run and save the notebook. Passing
those checks alone does not guarantee a useful artifact. Committed cells should
still be readable, rerunnable, and editable.

Make durable edits that reuse the notebook's existing names, imports,
dependencies, and UI model. Don't be lazy. Avoid one-off workarounds that pass
`cm` validation but leave a brittle notebook.

### Cell Bodies

Submit the code that belongs in the cell.

- **Submit cell contents** - `create_cell` and `edit_cell` take cell contents,
  not saved-file `@app.cell` wrappers.
- **Read before replacing** - for now, another editor may change a cell between
  scratchpad calls. Before `edit_cell`, read the current body from
  `ctx.cells[...]` and submit the full replacement.
- **Reuse notebook imports** - if `np` already exists, use it or edit the owning
  import cell. DO NOT add `import numpy as _np` just to bypass the graph.
- **Define public names intentionally** - use public names for values later
  cells should reference. Use private `_name` bindings or function locals for
  same-cell intermediates.
- **Define each public name once** - a public name has one owning cell.
  Reassigning it in another cell fails with `Multiply-defined names`; edit the
  owning cell or give the result a new name. See
  [gotchas.md](reference/gotchas.md).
- **Run cells deliberately** - `create_cell` and `edit_cell` change structure
  only. Queue `ctx.run_cell(...)` when the cell should execute.

### Prefer `cm`-Managed Changes

Use `cm` APIs when they exist. Avoid direct file edits, shell package commands,
and scratchpad-only state for changes that should persist.

- **Do not edit the `.py` artifact** - DO NOT use `Edit`, `Write`, or
  `NotebookEdit` on the notebook file during a live session. Use
  `ctx.edit_cell(...)` even for small changes.
- **Manage packages through `cm`** - use `ctx.packages.add()` or
  `ctx.packages.remove()` instead of direct `uv` or `pip`; confirm
  non-obvious dependency changes.
- **Avoid transient paths** - persisted cells should not depend on `/tmp/...`
  unless the work is intentionally transient.
- **Delete deliberately** - deleting a cell removes globals it defines. Reuse
  empty cells when convenient and delete cells left empty after edits.

### UI and Widgets

Inspect the object before changing it. Different UI objects update through
different paths.

- **Set `mo.ui.*` through `cm`** - use `ctx.set_ui_value(element, value)` inside
  `cm.get_context()`.
- **Set anywidget traitlets directly** - synced traitlets are Python
  attributes, for example `widget.value = 5`.

For designing custom visual or interactive output, see
[rich-representations.md](reference/rich-representations.md).

## References

- [execution-context.md](reference/execution-context.md) — scripts, MCP, auth, startup, and shell quoting
- [finding-marimo.md](reference/finding-marimo.md) — choosing the right marimo invocation
- [gotchas.md](reference/gotchas.md) — name redefinition, cached module proxies, and notebook traps
- [rich-representations.md](reference/rich-representations.md) — custom widgets and visualizations
- [notebook-improvements.md](reference/notebook-improvements.md) — improving existing notebooks

leading underscore.

```python
# Public definitions: values, total, i, value, mean
values = np.array([1, 2, 3])
total = 0
for i, value in enumerate(values):
    total += value
mean = total / len(values)
mean
```

```python
# Public definition: mean
_values = np.array([1, 2, 3])
_total = 0
for _i, _value in enumerate(_values):
    _total += _value
mean = _total / len(_values)
mean
```

Use private names for intermediates that no other cell should read. Public
names define the notebook-level dataflow. If a `cm` edit violates the contract,
marimo rejects the structural change and returns the validation error.

## The Notebook's Shape

A notebook is an ordered collection of cells. `ctx.cells` is the document view
and `ctx.graph` is the dataflow view.

```python
for cell in ctx.cells:
    cell  # .id, .code, .name, .config, .status, .errors

ctx.cells["setup"]         # by name
ctx.cells[0]               # by position
list(ctx.cells.keys())     # all IDs, in notebook order
```

Cell IDs are opaque strings which can be queried from the notebook or captured
from `cm` return values:

```python
cid = ctx.create_cell("df = pd.read_csv('data.csv')")
print(cid)   # e.g. 'Hbol'
```

Alternatively, cells can be assigned and referenced by `name`. The graph can be
used to understand its role in the dataflow.

```python
for cid, impl in ctx.graph.cells.items():
    impl  # .defs, .refs   (sets of public names)

ctx.graph.descendants(cid)   # cells that re-run when this one changes
ctx.graph.ancestors(cid)     # cells this one depends on
```

In marimo, deletes are *destructive* so it can be useful to query the
descendants prior to deleting to understand it's impact.

## Writing Notebook Changes

The graph contract keeps marimo able to run and save the notebook. Passing
those checks alone does not guarantee a useful artifact. Committed cells should
still be readable, rerunnable, and editable.

Make durable edits that reuse the notebook's existing names, imports,
dependencies, and UI model. Don't be lazy. Avoid one-off workarounds that pass
`cm` validation but leave a brittle notebook.

### Cell Bodies

Submit the code that belongs in the cell.

- **Submit cell contents** - `create_cell` and `edit_cell` take cell contents,
  not saved-file `@app.cell` wrappers.
- **Read before replacing** - for now, another editor may change a cell between
  scratchpad calls. Before `edit_cell`, read the current body from
  `ctx.cells[...]` and submit the full replacement.
- **Reuse notebook imports** - if `np` already exists, use it or edit the owning
  import cell. DO NOT add `import numpy as _np` just to bypass the graph.
- **Define public names intentionally** - use public names for values later
  cells should reference. Use private `_name` bindings or function locals for
  same-cell intermediates.
- **Define each public name once** - a public name has one owning cell.
  Reassigning it in another cell fails with `Multiply-defined names`; edit the
  owning cell or give the result a new name. See
  [gotchas.md](reference/gotchas.md).
- **Run cells deliberately** - `create_cell` and `edit_cell` change structure
  only. Queue `ctx.run_cell(...)` when the cell should execute.

### Prefer `cm`-Managed Changes

Use `cm` APIs when they exist. Avoid direct file edits, shell package commands,
and scratchpad-only state for changes that should persist.

- **Do not edit the `.py` artifact** - DO NOT use `Edit`, `Write`, or
  `NotebookEdit` on the notebook file during a live session. Use
  `ctx.edit_cell(...)` even for small changes.
- **Manage packages through `cm`** - use `ctx.packages.add()` or
  `ctx.packages.remove()` instead of direct `uv` or `pip`; confirm
  non-obvious dependency changes.
- **Avoid transient paths** - persisted cells should not depend on `/tmp/...`
  unless the work is intentionally transient.
- **Delete deliberately** - deleting a cell removes globals it defines. Reuse
  empty cells when convenient and delete cells left empty after edits.

### UI and Widgets

Inspect the object before changing it. Different UI objects update through
different paths.

- **Set `mo.ui.*` through `cm`** - use `ctx.set_ui_value(element, value)` inside
  `cm.get_context()`.
- **Set anywidget traitlets directly** - synced traitlets are Python
  attributes, for example `widget.value = 5`.

For designing custom visual or interactive output, see
[rich-representations.md](reference/rich-representations.md).

## References

- [execution-context.md](reference/execution-context.md) — scripts, MCP, auth, startup, and shell quoting
- [finding-marimo.md](reference/finding-marimo.md) — choosing the right marimo invocation
- [gotchas.md](reference/gotchas.md) — name redefinition, cached module proxies, and notebook traps
- [rich-representations.md](reference/rich-representations.md) — custom widgets and visualizations
- [notebook-improvements.md](reference/notebook-improvements.md) — improving existing notebooks

import marimo._code_mode as cm
from pathlib import Path

namespace = {}
exec(Path('/tmp/html_evaluation_cells.py').read_text(encoding='utf-8'), namespace)
cell_sources = {
    'html_eval_scope': namespace['scope_code'],
    'html_eval_setup': namespace['setup_code'],
    'html_eval_controls': namespace['controls_code'],
    'html_eval_run': namespace['run_code'],
    'html_eval_report': namespace['report_code'],
}

async with cm.get_context() as ctx:
    for name, source in cell_sources.items():
        existing = next((cell for cell in ctx.cells if cell.name == name), None)
        cell_id = existing.id if existing else ctx.create_cell(source, name=name, hide_code=True)
        if existing:
            ctx.edit_cell(cell_id, code=source)
        ctx.run_cell(cell_id)
        print(f'{name}: {cell_id}')

report_code = r'''if html_eval_result is None:
    html_eval_report = mo.md(
        "## HTML Extraction Comparison\nNo evaluation output is available."
    )
else:
    import json as _report_json
    from urllib.parse import urlparse as _report_urlparse

    _html_eval_summary_rows = [
        {"metric": "dataset", "value": html_eval_result["dataset"]},
        {"metric": "revision", "value": html_eval_result["revision"]},
        {"metric": "selection source", "value": html_eval_result["selection_source"]},
        {"metric": "documents", "value": f"{html_eval_result['documents']:,}"},
        {"metric": "raw HTML characters", "value": f"{html_eval_result['raw_html_characters']:,}"},
        {"metric": "supplied reference-text characters", "value": f"{html_eval_result['reference_text_characters']:,}"},
    ]
    _html_eval_trace_rows = []
    with HTML_EVAL_DOCUMENT_METRICS_PATH.open(encoding="utf-8") as _trace_handle:
        for _trace_line in _trace_handle:
            if len(_html_eval_trace_rows) == 3:
                break
            _trace = _report_json.loads(_trace_line)
            _trace_rows = _trace["techniques"]
            _html_eval_trace_rows.append({
                "source index": _trace["source_index"],
                "source host": _report_urlparse(_trace["url"] or "").netloc,
                "raw HTML chars": _trace["raw_html_characters"],
                "reference chars": _trace["reference_characters"],
                "residual chars": _trace_rows["residual_markup"]["output_characters"],
                "block-density chars": _trace_rows["block_density"]["output_characters"],
                "semantic-DOM chars": _trace_rows["semantic_dom"]["output_characters"],
                "layout chars": _trace_rows["layout_renderer"]["output_characters"],
                "JSON-LD chars": _trace_rows["jsonld_metadata"]["output_characters"],
            })
    _html_eval_notes = (
        "### Interpretation\n"
        "All executed rows are transparent local implementations of the named technique family; they are **not** claimed to be the external libraries. "
        "The external adapters are listed separately because the active marimo kernel lacks those dependencies. "
        "Reference-token overlap is agreement with the supplied C4 text, not a human quality score. "
        "`jsonld_metadata` extracts metadata rather than article prose, so its character-retention figures are not comparable to main-content extractors."
    )
    html_eval_report = mo.vstack(
        [
            mo.md("## HTML Extraction Comparison"),
            mo.ui.table(_html_eval_summary_rows),
            mo.md("### Document-Level Extraction Trace\nThe trace reports structural output measurements only; raw page content is not displayed."),
            mo.ui.table(_html_eval_trace_rows),
            mo.md("### Unified Technique Metrics"),
            mo.ui.table(html_eval_result["metrics"]),
            mo.md(_html_eval_notes),
            mo.md(
                f"**Artifacts:** manifest `{html_eval_result['manifest_path']}` · aggregate metrics `{html_eval_result['metrics_path']}` · document-level metrics `{html_eval_result['document_metrics_path']}`"
            ),
        ]
    )
html_eval_report'''

Implemented an auxiliary HTML extraction evaluation in `stepwise_cleaning.py` at **http://127.0.0.1:2720**.

## Corpus

Downloaded and cached a deterministic 30-document HTML subset from:

- Dataset: [`bs-modeling-metadata/c4-en-html-with-metadata`](https://huggingface.co/datasets/bs-modeling-metadata/c4-en-html-with-metadata)
- Revision: `d7fa66c5f9686a055f50dbdaeb0d8950209cf0f8`
- Split: `train`

The dataset retains actual `html`, `url`, and supplied `text` fields.

Artifacts:

```text
data/c4_en_html_evaluation/raw_html.jsonl
data/c4_en_html_evaluation/impl/selection_manifest.json
data/c4_en_html_evaluation/impl/technique_metrics.json
data/c4_en_html_evaluation/impl/document_metrics.jsonl
```

Verification: all 30 cached records contain non-empty raw HTML; all 30 have document-level extraction metrics.

## Executed comparison

The notebook now includes:

- **Auxiliary HTML Extraction Evaluation Corpus** — scope and validity boundary.
- A bounded download/execution control.
- A **Document-Level Extraction Trace** for three source documents, showing only structural measurements—not page text.
- A single paginated **Unified Technique Metrics** table at the end.

### Measured results

| Technique family | Implementation | Documents | Mean output chars | Output / raw HTML | Mean C4-reference token overlap |
|---|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Residual markup removal | Transparent `HTMLParser` baseline | 30 | 5,304.6 | 9.276% | 96.15% |
| Block-density selection | jusText-style local implementation | 30 | 2,418.7 | 4.229% | 65.26% |
| Semantic DOM scoring | Readability/Trafilatura-family local implementation | 30 | 2,770.3 | 4.844% | 70.70% |
| Layout-preserving rendering | Inscriptis-style local implementation | 30 | 11,082.5 | 19.379% | 96.15% |
| Structured JSON-LD extraction | extruct-style local implementation | 30 | 12.2 | 0.021% | 0.40% |

Aggregate input:

```text
30 documents
1,715,638 raw HTML characters
110,039 supplied C4 reference-text characters
```

Interpretation:

- Residual and layout-preserving renderers retain substantially more text, including navigation, repeated layout text, and non-article content.
- Block-density and semantic-DOM approaches produce shorter candidate main-content outputs.
- JSON-LD is metadata extraction, not article-text extraction; its retention metrics are intentionally not comparable to main-content methods.
- The C4 `text` field is used only as an **agreement proxy**. It is not a human-labeled extraction-quality ground truth.

## External-library status

I requested the named extraction dependencies through marimo’s package manager, but the active virtual environment lacks `pip`; imports remained unavailable. The unified table therefore explicitly records these as **not executed**, rather than claiming they ran:

- Trafilatura
- jusText
- Inscriptis
- Resiliparse
- extruct
- readability-lxml

It also records:

- MinerU-HTML / AICC — model/runtime unavailable; no Hindi-quality claim.
- SCRIBES — no runtime; additionally requires same-site page groups.

The five executed rows are labeled as transparent local implementations of the technique **families**, not substitutes for the unavailable external libraries.

## Verification

- Browser verified the document-level trace, executed-family rows, unified metric table, and technique-status rows.
- Notebook health check: all 24 live cells idle with no errors.

---
name: marimo-pair
description: >-
  Drive a live marimo notebook as a workspace: run Python in the same kernel
  the user does, inspect live notebook state, and commit durable notebook
  changes. Use when the user wants to start a marimo notebook or pair on an
  active marimo session.
allowed-tools: Bash(bash **/scripts/discover-servers.sh *), Bash(bash **/scripts/execute-code.sh *), Read
---

marimo is a reactive Python runtime for building reproducible Python programs
(marimo notebooks). Cells are connected by the variables they define and
reference. Running a cell re-executes dependents in dataflow order. The active
runtime holds the kernel namespace, cell state, and dataflow graph. The
notebook (`.py` file) is the artifact the kernel writes from that state while a
session is running.

A user interacts with the same runtime via a notebook UI with cells, outputs,
and widgets.

**WARNING. The active runtime is the source of truth.** During a session, you
SHOULD NOT modify the associated `.py` file directly. File edits WILL NOT reach
the active kernel or user, and the kernel may overwrite them on save. Use
`marimo._code_mode` (`cm`) for notebook changes. Reading disk is fine, but
prefer `ctx.cells[...].code` for current cell code.

## Connect to a Notebook

Use the bundled script (`bash scripts/execute-code.sh`) or MCP
(`execute_code(...)`) to run Python in a live marimo kernel.

If the user provides a notebook URL, target it directly:

```bash
bash scripts/execute-code.sh --url http://localhost:2718 -c "print('connected')"
```

Use `-c` only for short one-liners. For multiline code or code containing
quotes, backticks, `$`, or braces, use a single-quoted heredoc:

```bash
bash scripts/execute-code.sh --url http://localhost:2718 <<'PY'
import marimo._code_mode as cm

async with cm.get_context() as ctx:
    cid = ctx.create_cell("x = df.head()")
    ctx.run_cell(cid)
PY
```

When code already lives in a file, pass the file path:

```bash
bash scripts/execute-code.sh --url http://localhost:2718 /tmp/code.py
```

If no target is provided, find or start a session. First look for a running
session with `bash scripts/discover-servers.sh`, MCP `list_sessions()`, or
local process context. When multiple sessions are possible, target with
`--url`, `--port`, or `--session`.

If no server is running and the user wants a notebook, start marimo with
`--no-token` (and without `--headless`) so it auto-registers for discovery. The
notebook UI must be open before there is an active session for `execute-code`
to target. The right way to invoke marimo depends on context (project tooling,
global install, sandbox mode). If the notebook file contains a PEP 723 `#
/// script` header, it MUST be opened with `--sandbox` — otherwise marimo
ignores the inline dependencies. See
[finding-marimo.md](reference/finding-marimo.md) for the full decision tree and
[execution-context.md](reference/execution-context.md) for scripts, MCP, and
shell quoting.

## Scratchpad Scope

`execute-code` evaluates Python in marimo's scratchpad: a temporary namespace
with a shallow copy of the kernel globals. Notebook variables are available by
name, but new top-level bindings and rebindings are discarded after each call.
In-place mutations to notebook-owned objects can persist because those names
still reference live objects.

Each call reports stdout and stderr from the scratchpad, plus console output
from notebook cells it causes to run, including reactive descendants.

### Ordinary Python

Use ordinary Python in the scratchpad to inspect variables, sample data, test
transformations, probe APIs, check imports, and read widget state.

```python
print(df.head())

x = 10
print(x)
```

Here `df` comes from notebook globals, while `x` is a scratchpad-local binding.
`x` exists for this call only and WILL NOT be added to notebook globals.

### Persist with `cm`

Top-level scratchpad assignments and rebindings are temporary. To persist work,
including new variables, you MUST submit changes through `marimo._code_mode`
(`cm`).

`marimo._code_mode` is a PRIVATE, UNSTABLE agent API (note the leading
underscore). It exists for tools like this skill to drive a live kernel from
the scratchpad. DO NOT import it from notebook cells, library code, or
anything a user would run — methods can change or disappear across marimo
versions and kernels. Treat every `import marimo._code_mode as cm` as
scratchpad-only.

At session start, inspect what `cm` exposes in the active kernel:

```python
import marimo._code_mode as cm

help(cm)
```

Open a code-mode context to queue notebook changes.

```python
import marimo._code_mode as cm

async with cm.get_context() as ctx:
    cid = ctx.create_cell("x = df.head()")
    ctx.run_cell(cid)
```

The scratchpad supports top-level async code. Use `async with` directly;
wrapping it in `asyncio.run(...)` is unnecessary and can conflict with the
kernel's event loop.

After this block exits and the new cell runs, `x` is notebook state. Later
scratchpad calls can read `x` by name. Code later in the same scratchpad call
should read `ctx.globals["x"]`, because the scratchpad namespace was copied
before the cell ran.

Inside the context, queued mutation methods are synchronous. Call them
directly; do not `await` them. Each call queues an operation for marimo to
apply when the context exits normally. If the block raises, the queue is
discarded.

On clean exit, marimo applies packages, validates and applies structural cell
changes, runs queued cells, then may run dependents. Validation is only
structural since queued cell runs can still error. `create_cell` and
`edit_cell` change notebook structure only. Use `run_cell` to execute. 

`create_cell` currently defaults to `hide_code=True`, which collapses the code
editor in the UI. Pass `hide_code=False` if the user wants created cells to
be visible without manually expanding them.


## Marimo Rules

marimo imposes a small contract on notebook code so it can keep the notebook as
a directed acyclic graph (DAG):

- **No cycles** - cells cannot depend on each other in a cycle.
- **No public redefinitions across cells** - each name has one owning cell.
- **No wildcard imports** - `import *` prevents static analysis of definitions.

These rules keep the kernel, UI, and saved artifact consistent.

When `cm` submits a cell body, marimo parses its top-level definitions and
references. A top-level name enters the graph unless it is private with a
leading underscore.

```python
# Public definitions: values, total, i, value, mean
values = np.array([1, 2, 3])
total = 0
for i, value in enumerate(values):
    total += value
mean = total / len(values)
mean
```

```python
# Public definition: mean
_values = np.array([1, 2, 3])
_total = 0
for _i, _value in enumerate(_values):
    _total += _value
mean = _total / len(_values)
mean
```

Use private names for intermediates that no other cell should read. Public
names define the notebook-level dataflow. If a `cm` edit violates the contract,
marimo rejects the structural change and returns the validation error.

## The Notebook's Shape

A notebook is an ordered collection of cells. `ctx.cells` is the document view
and `ctx.graph` is the dataflow view.

```python
for cell in ctx.cells:
    cell  # .id, .code, .name, .config, .status, .errors

ctx.cells["setup"]         # by name
ctx.cells[0]               # by position
list(ctx.cells.keys())     # all IDs, in notebook order
```

Cell IDs are opaque strings which can be queried from the notebook or captured
from `cm` return values:

```python
cid = ctx.create_cell("df = pd.read_csv('data.csv')")
print(cid)   # e.g. 'Hbol'
```

Alternatively, cells can be assigned and referenced by `name`. The graph can be
used to understand its role in the dataflow.

```python
for cid, impl in ctx.graph.cells.items():
    impl  # .defs, .refs   (sets of public names)

ctx.graph.descendants(cid)   # cells that re-run when this one changes
ctx.graph.ancestors(cid)     # cells this one depends on
```

In marimo, deletes are *destructive* so it can be useful to query the
descendants prior to deleting to understand it's impact.

## Writing Notebook Changes

The graph contract keeps marimo able to run and save the notebook. Passing
those checks alone does not guarantee a useful artifact. Committed cells should
still be readable, rerunnable, and editable.

Make durable edits that reuse the notebook's existing names, imports,
dependencies, and UI model. Don't be lazy. Avoid one-off workarounds that pass
`cm` validation but leave a brittle notebook.

### Cell Bodies

Submit the code that belongs in the cell.

- **Submit cell contents** - `create_cell` and `edit_cell` take cell contents,
  not saved-file `@app.cell` wrappers.
- **Read before replacing** - for now, another editor may change a cell between
  scratchpad calls. Before `edit_cell`, read the current body from
  `ctx.cells[...]` and submit the full replacement.
- **Reuse notebook imports** - if `np` already exists, use it or edit the owning
  import cell. DO NOT add `import numpy as _np` just to bypass the graph.
- **Define public names intentionally** - use public names for values later
  cells should reference. Use private `_name` bindings or function locals for
  same-cell intermediates.
- **Define each public name once** - a public name has one owning cell.
  Reassigning it in another cell fails with `Multiply-defined names`; edit the

  only. Queue `ctx.run_cell(...)` when the cell should execute.

and scratchpad-only state for changes that should persist.

- **Do not edit the `.py` artifact** - DO NOT use `Edit`, `Write`, or
  `NotebookEdit` on the notebook file during a live session. Use
  `ctx.edit_cell(...)` even for small changes.

  `ctx.packages.remove()` instead of direct `uv` or `pip`; confirm
  non-obvious dependency changes.

  unless the work is intentionally transient.

---
name: marimo-pair
description: >-
  Drive a live marimo notebook as a workspace: run Python in the same kernel
  the user does, inspect live notebook state, and commit durable notebook
  changes. Use when the user wants to start a marimo notebook or pair on an
  active marimo session.
allowed-tools: Bash(bash **/scripts/discover-servers.sh *), Bash(bash **/scripts/execute-code.sh *), Read
---

marimo is a reactive Python runtime for building reproducible Python programs
(marimo notebooks). Cells are connected by the variables they define and
reference. Running a cell re-executes dependents in dataflow order. The active
runtime holds the kernel namespace, cell state, and dataflow graph. The
notebook (`.py` file) is the artifact the kernel writes from that state while a
session is running.

A user interacts with the same runtime via a notebook UI with cells, outputs,
and widgets.

**WARNING. The active runtime is the source of truth.** During a session, you
SHOULD NOT modify the associated `.py` file directly. File edits WILL NOT reach
the active kernel or user, and the kernel may overwrite them on save. Use
`marimo._code_mode` (`cm`) for notebook changes. Reading disk is fine, but
prefer `ctx.cells[...].code` for current cell code.

## Connect to a Notebook

Use the bundled script (`bash scripts/execute-code.sh`) or MCP
(`execute_code(...)`) to run Python in a live marimo kernel.

If the user provides a notebook URL, target it directly:

```bash
bash scripts/execute-code.sh --url http://localhost:2718 -c "print('connected')"
```

Use `-c` only for short one-liners. For multiline code or code containing
quotes, backticks, `$`, or braces, use a single-quoted heredoc:

```bash
bash scripts/execute-code.sh --url http://localhost:2718 <<'PY'
import marimo._code_mode as cm

async with cm.get_context() as ctx:
    cid = ctx.create_cell("x = df.head()")
    ctx.run_cell(cid)
PY
```

When code already lives in a file, pass the file path:

```bash
bash scripts/execute-code.sh --url http://localhost:2718 /tmp/code.py
```

If no target is provided, find or start a session. First look for a running
session with `bash scripts/discover-servers.sh`, MCP `list_sessions()`, or
local process context. When multiple sessions are possible, target with
`--url`, `--port`, or `--session`.

If no server is running and the user wants a notebook, start marimo with
`--no-token` (and without `--headless`) so it auto-registers for discovery. The
notebook UI must be open before there is an active session for `execute-code`
to target. The right way to invoke marimo depends on context (project tooling,
global install, sandbox mode). If the notebook file contains a PEP 723 `#
/// script` header, it MUST be opened with `--sandbox` — otherwise marimo
ignores the inline dependencies. See
[finding-marimo.md](reference/finding-marimo.md) for the full decision tree and
[execution-context.md](reference/execution-context.md) for scripts, MCP, and
shell quoting.

## Scratchpad Scope

`execute-code` evaluates Python in marimo's scratchpad: a temporary namespace
with a shallow copy of the kernel globals. Notebook variables are available by
name, but new top-level bindings and rebindings are discarded after each call.
In-place mutations to notebook-owned objects can persist because those names
still reference live objects.

Each call reports stdout and stderr from the scratchpad, plus console output
from notebook cells it causes to run, including reactive descendants.

### Ordinary Python

Use ordinary Python in the scratchpad to inspect variables, sample data, test
transformations, probe APIs, check imports, and read widget state.

```python
print(df.head())

x = 10
print(x)
```

Here `df` comes from notebook globals, while `x` is a scratchpad-local binding.
`x` exists for this call only and WILL NOT be added to notebook globals.

### Persist with `cm`

Top-level scratchpad assignments and rebindings are temporary. To persist work,
including new variables, you MUST submit changes through `marimo._code_mode`
(`cm`).

`marimo._code_mode` is a PRIVATE, UNSTABLE agent API (note the leading
underscore). It exists for tools like this skill to drive a live kernel from
the scratchpad. DO NOT import it from notebook cells, library code, or
anything a user would run — methods can change or disappear across marimo
versions and kernels. Treat every `import marimo._code_mode as cm` as
scratchpad-only.

At session start, inspect what `cm` exposes in the active kernel:

```python
import marimo._code_mode as cm

help(cm)
```

Open a code-mode context to queue notebook changes.

```python
import marimo._code_mode as cm

async with cm.get_context() as ctx:
    cid = ctx.create_cell("x = df.head()")
    ctx.run_cell(cid)
```

The scratchpad supports top-level async code. Use `async with` directly;
wrapping it in `asyncio.run(...)` is unnecessary and can conflict with the
kernel's event loop.

After this block exits and the new cell runs, `x` is notebook state. Later
scratchpad calls can read `x` by name. Code later in the same scratchpad call
should read `ctx.globals["x"]`, because the scratchpad namespace was copied
before the cell ran.

Inside the context, queued mutation methods are synchronous. Call them
directly; do not `await` them. Each call queues an operation for marimo to
apply when the context exits normally. If the block raises, the queue is
discarded.

On clean exit, marimo applies packages, validates and applies structural cell
changes, runs queued cells, then may run dependents. Validation is only
structural since queued cell runs can still error. `create_cell` and
`edit_cell` change notebook structure only. Use `run_cell` to execute. 

`create_cell` currently defaults to `hide_code=True`, which collapses the code
editor in the UI. Pass `hide_code=False` if the user wants created cells to
be visible without manually expanding them.


## Marimo Rules

marimo imposes a small contract on notebook code so it can keep the notebook as
a directed acyclic graph (DAG):

- **No cycles** - cells cannot depend on each other in a cycle.
- **No public redefinitions across cells** - each name has one owning cell.
- **No wildcard imports** - `import *` prevents static analysis of definitions.

These rules keep the kernel, UI, and saved artifact consistent.

When `cm` submits a cell body, marimo parses its top-level definitions and
references. A top-level name enters the graph unless it is private with a
leading underscore.

```python
# Public definitions: values, total, i, value, mean
values = np.array([1, 2, 3])
total = 0
for i, value in enumerate(values):
    total += value
mean = total / len(values)
mean
```

```python
# Public definition: mean
_values = np.array([1, 2, 3])
_total = 0
for _i, _value in enumerate(_values):
    _total += _value
mean = _total / len(_values)
mean
```

Use private names for intermediates that no other cell should read. Public
names define the notebook-level dataflow. If a `cm` edit violates the contract,
marimo rejects the structural change and returns the validation error.

## The Notebook's Shape

A notebook is an ordered collection of cells. `ctx.cells` is the document view
and `ctx.graph` is the dataflow view.

```python
for cell in ctx.cells:
    cell  # .id, .code, .name, .config, .status, .errors

ctx.cells["setup"]         # by name
ctx.cells[0]               # by position
list(ctx.cells.keys())     # all IDs, in notebook order
```

Cell IDs are opaque strings which can be queried from the notebook or captured
from `cm` return values:

```python
cid = ctx.create_cell("df = pd.read_csv('data.csv')")
print(cid)   # e.g. 'Hbol'
```

Alternatively, cells can be assigned and referenced by `name`. The graph can be
used to understand its role in the dataflow.

```python
for cid, impl in ctx.graph.cells.items():
    impl  # .defs, .refs   (sets of public names)

ctx.graph.descendants(cid)   # cells that re-run when this one changes
ctx.graph.ancestors(cid)     # cells this one depends on
```

In marimo, deletes are *destructive* so it can be useful to query the
descendants prior to deleting to understand it's impact.

## Writing Notebook Changes

The graph contract keeps marimo able to run and save the notebook. Passing
those checks alone does not guarantee a useful artifact. Committed cells should
still be readable, rerunnable, and editable.

Make durable edits that reuse the notebook's existing names, imports,
dependencies, and UI model. Don't be lazy. Avoid one-off workarounds that pass
`cm` validation but leave a brittle notebook.

### Cell Bodies

Submit the code that belongs in the cell.

- **Submit cell contents** - `create_cell` and `edit_cell` take cell contents,
  not saved-file `@app.cell` wrappers.
- **Read before replacing** - for now, another editor may change a cell between
  scratchpad calls. Before `edit_cell`, read the current body from
  `ctx.cells[...]` and submit the full replacement.
- **Reuse notebook imports** - if `np` already exists, use it or edit the owning
  import cell. DO NOT add `import numpy as _np` just to bypass the graph.
- **Define public names intentionally** - use public names for values later
  cells should reference. Use private `_name` bindings or function locals for
  same-cell intermediates.
- **Define each public name once** - a public name has one owning cell.
  Reassigning it in another cell fails with `Multiply-defined names`; edit the
  owning cell or give the result a new name. See
  [gotchas.md](reference/gotchas.md).
- **Run cells deliberately** - `create_cell` and `edit_cell` change structure
  only. Queue `ctx.run_cell(...)` when the cell should execute.

### Prefer `cm`-Managed Changes

Use `cm` APIs when they exist. Avoid direct file edits, shell package commands,
and scratchpad-only state for changes that should persist.

- **Do not edit the `.py` artifact** - DO NOT use `Edit`, `Write`, or
  `NotebookEdit` on the notebook file during a live session. Use
  `ctx.edit_cell(...)` even for small changes.
- **Manage packages through `cm`** - use `ctx.packages.add()` or
  `ctx.packages.remove()` instead of direct `uv` or `pip`; confirm
  non-obvious dependency changes.
- **Avoid transient paths** - persisted cells should not depend on `/tmp/...`
  unless the work is intentionally transient.
- **Delete deliberately** - deleting a cell removes globals it defines. Reuse
  empty cells when convenient and delete cells left empty after edits.

### UI and Widgets

Inspect the object before changing it. Different UI objects update through
different paths.

- **Set `mo.ui.*` through `cm`** - use `ctx.set_ui_value(element, value)` inside
  `cm.get_context()`.
- **Set anywidget traitlets directly** - synced traitlets are Python
  attributes, for example `widget.value = 5`.

For designing custom visual or interactive output, see
[rich-representations.md](reference/rich-representations.md).

## References

- [execution-context.md](reference/execution-context.md) — scripts, MCP, auth, startup, and shell quoting
- [finding-marimo.md](reference/finding-marimo.md) — choosing the right marimo invocation
- [gotchas.md](reference/gotchas.md) — name redefinition, cached module proxies, and notebook traps
- [rich-representations.md](reference/rich-representations.md) — custom widgets and visualizations
- [notebook-improvements.md](reference/notebook-improvements.md) — improving existing notebooks

It transforms their text by removing markup, explicit web boilerplate, and layout whitespace.█¶user:dive deep into extraction techniques which we can use for hindi datasets█## TL;DR█Effective extraction for Indic languages involves balancing heuristic-based tools like Boilerpipe and JusText with modern model-based pipelines. Techniques include pixel-level analysis, layout-aware conversion, and semantic categorization to preserve structured data and handle orthographic script complexity.█----█## Heuristic and traditional extraction tools█Traditional web content extraction often relies on established heuristic-based libraries, which remain common in many Indic language datasets. For instance, the Humkinar project, which targets the low-resource Urdu language, utilizes Boilerpipe and JusText for main content extraction from Common Crawl datasets [1]. Similarly, Inscriptis is highlighted as a layout-aware Python library that improves upon traditional tools like JusText, HTML2text, and Lynx by preserving spatial alignment, which is critical for knowledge extraction tasks [2]. These libraries are often integrated into broader data pipelines that include language identification, deduplication, and filtering steps to ensure high-quality monolingual output [3].█----█## Emerging model-based extraction approaches█Recent research suggests that shifting from density-based heuristics to model-based extraction significantly improves data quality for large language models. The MinerU-HTML pipeline reformulates extraction as a sequence labeling problem using a 0.6B-parameter language model [4]. This approach categorizes semantic elements before conversion to Markdown, achieving 81.8% ROUGE-N F1 compared to 63.6% for Trafilatura [4]. Furthermore, the SCRIBES framework utilizes reinforcement learning to generate reusable extraction scripts based on layout similarity across webpages, which is particularly effective for semi-structured data like tables and lists [5].█----█## Challenges in Indic language processing█Indic languages present unique challenges due to script diversity, orthographic complexity, and the need for concept-based analysis. Research has explored pixel-level addressing of web content, which is subsequently reduced to numerical equivalents via matrix manipulations to accommodate the variations in Indian text [6]. This approach aims to create a generic model that can integrate with existing data mining tools [6]. Additionally, for languages like Marathi and Urdu, researchers emphasize the necessity of specialized URL selection algorithms and customized parsers to handle the specific linguistic and structural vagaries of regional web documents [1] [7].█| Technique | Primary Mechanism | Key Advantage |█| :--- | :--- | :--- |█| **Boilerpipe / JusText** | Heuristic/Density-based | Low resource usage; widely available [1] |█| **Inscriptis** | Layout-aware conversion | Preserves spatial structure [2] |█| **MinerU-HTML** | Model-based sequence labeling | Superior structure preservation [4] |█| **SCRIBES** | Reinforcement learning | Reusable scripts for structures [5] |█| **Pixel-level analysis** | Matrix manipulation | Handles varied regional scripts [6] |█----█## Comprehensive curation pipelines█Effective datasets for Indic languages require a multifaceted pipeline that incorporates crawling, cleaning, and deduplication [8]. Projects such as IndicLLMSuite utilize a clean, open-source pipeline to curate pre-training data from diverse web, PDF, and video sources [8]. Beyond basic extraction, these workflows often include specialized post-processing, such as profanity assessment, topic classification, and the calculation of website quality scores, to ensure the resulting dataset is suitable for training high-quality language models [8] [1].█and█Analyzing techniques and papers for Hindi LLM data extraction█I have analyzed the search results and web content to identify the most robust techniques for the "Extract" stage, particularly for Hindi datasets. Recommended "Bulletproof" Tools█For a production-grade pipeline, you should move beyond naive tag stripping. The state-of-the-art involves tools that understand both text density and DOM structure:█Trafilatura: Currently considered the industry standard for heuristic extraction. It is highly effective at removing sidebars and navigation while preserving the main text. It performs well on Hindi news sites and blogs.█Inscriptis: Excellent for layout-aware conversion. If your Hindi dataset includes tables or structured lists (common in government portals or educational sites), Inscriptis ensures that the spatial relationships are preserved rather than flattened into a single line.█Resiliparse: Part of the ChatNoir/Common Crawl ecosystem. It is extremely fast and robust for large-scale extraction from raw WARC files, often used as the first pass in massive pipelines.█2. Modern Model-Based Extraction (The "AICC" Approach)█Recent research (late 2024-2025) suggests that for maximum accuracy (yielding your "bulletproof" result), you should treat extraction as a sequence labeling task.█MinerU-HTML / AICC: These models (e.g., the 0.6B parameter MinerU) categorize every HTML element (e.g., "article-body", "title", "boilerplate") before converting to text. This reduces the error rate where legal text or "related articles" are accidentally merged into the main content.█Key Advantage for Hindi: Many Hindi news sites use complex, nested div structures with multiple ad-wrappers. A model-based parser is significantly better at distinguishing between a Hindi "Recommended for you" snippet and the actual article text than a simple density heuristic.█3. def _html_normalize(value):
    return _html_re.sub(r"\s+", " ", value or " ").strip()

def _html_tokens(value):
    return set(
        token.lower() for token in _HTML_EVAL_TOKEN.findall(value or "")
    )

def _html_overlap(candidate, reference):
    candidate_tokens = _html_tokens(candidate)
    reference_tokens = _html_tokens(reference)
    if not candidate_tokens or not reference_tokens:
        return 0.0
    return len(candidate_tokens & reference_tokens) / len(reference_tokens)

class _HtmlTextRenderer(_HTMLParser):
    def __init__(self, layout=False):
        super().__init__(convert_charrefs=True)
        self.parts = []
        self.layout = layout
        self.skip_depth = 0
        self.tag_count = 0

    def handle_starttag(self, tag, attrs):
        self.tag_count += 1
        if tag in _HTML_EVAL_SKIP_TAGS:
            self.skip_depth += 1
        if self.skip_depth == 0 and tag in _HTML_EVAL_BLOCK_TAGS:
            self.parts.append("\n" if self.layout else " ")

    def handle_endtag(self, tag):
        self.tag_count += 1
        if tag in _HTML_EVAL_SKIP_TAGS and self.skip_depth:
            self.skip_depth -= 1
        if self.skip_depth == 0 and tag in _HTML_EVAL_BLOCK_TAGS:
            self.parts.append("\n" if self.layout else " ")

    def handle_data(self, data):
        if self.skip_depth == 0:
            self.parts.append(data)

    def render(self):
        value = "".join(self.parts)
        return (
            _html_re.sub(r"\n{3,}", "\n\n", value).strip()
            if self.layout
            else _html_normalize(value)
        )

class _HtmlBlockCollector(_HTMLParser):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__(convert_charrefs=True)
        self.blocks = []
        self.current = None
        self.link_depth = 0
        self.skip_depth = 0

    def handle_starttag(self, tag, attrs):
        if tag in _HTML_EVAL_SKIP_TAGS:
            self.skip_depth += 1
        if self.skip_depth:
            return
        if tag == "a":
            self.link_depth += 1
        if tag in {
            "p",
            "li",
            "h1",
            "h2",
            "h3",
            "h4",
            "h5",
            "h6",
            "td",
            "th",
            "pre",
        }:
            if self.current:
                self._finish()
            self.current = {"tag": tag, "parts": [], "link_chars": 0}

    def handle_endtag(self, tag):
        if tag in _HTML_EVAL_SKIP_TAGS and self.skip_depth:
            self.skip_depth -= 1
            return
        if self.skip_depth:
            return
        if tag == "a" and self.link_depth:
            self.link_depth -= 1
        if self.current and tag == self.current["tag"]:
            self._finish()

    def handle_data(self, data):
        if self.skip_depth or not self.current:
            return
        self.current["parts"].append(data)
        if self.link_depth:
            self.current["link_chars"] += len(data)

    def close(self):
        super().close()
        if self.current:
            self._finish()

    def _finish(self):
        text = _html_normalize("".join(self.current["parts"]))
        if text:
            self.blocks.append(
                {
                    "text": text,
                    "link_ratio": self.current["link_chars"]
                    / max(1, len(text)),
                }
            )
        self.current = None

class _HtmlSemanticCollector(_HTMLParser):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__(convert_charrefs=True)
        self.candidates = []
        self.stack = []
        self.link_depth = 0
        self.skip_depth = 0

    def handle_starttag(self, tag, attrs):
        if tag in _HTML_EVAL_SKIP_TAGS:
            self.skip_depth += 1
        if self.skip_depth:
            return
        if tag == "a":
            self.link_depth += 1
        if tag in {"article", "main", "section", "div", "body"}:
            attr_map = dict(attrs)
            marker = " ".join(
                (attr_map.get("id", ""), attr_map.get("class", ""))
            ).lower()
            self.stack.append(
                {
                    "tag": tag,
                    "marker": marker,
                    "parts": [],
                    "link_chars": 0,
                }
            )

    def handle_endtag(self, tag):
        if tag in _HTML_EVAL_SKIP_TAGS and self.skip_depth:
            self.skip_depth -= 1
            return
        if self.skip_depth:
            return
        if tag == "a" and self.link_depth:
            self.link_depth -= 1
        if self.stack and tag == self.stack[-1]["tag"]:
            candidate = self.stack.pop()
            text = _html_normalize("".join(candidate["parts"]))
            if text:
                bonus = (
                    1200
                    if candidate["tag"] == "article"
                    else 900
                    if candidate["tag"] == "main"
                    else 0
                )
                if any(
                    key in candidate["marker"]
                    for key in (
                        "article",
                        "content",
                        "main",
                        "post",
                        "story",
                    )
                ):
                    bonus += 600
                penalty = candidate["link_chars"] * 4
                self.candidates.append(
                    {"text": text, "score": len(text) + bonus - penalty}
                )

    def handle_data(self, data):
        if self.skip_depth:
            return
        for candidate in self.stack:
            candidate["parts"].append(data)
            if self.link_depth:
                candidate["link_chars"] += len(data)

            block["text"]

                parser.blocks,
                key=lambda item: len(item["text"]),
                reverse=True,
            )[:3]
        ]
    return "\n\n".join(selected), {
        "candidate_blocks": len(parser.blocks),
        "selected_blocks": len(selected),
    }

def _html_semantic_extract(value):
    parser = _HtmlSemanticCollector()
    parser.feed(value)
    parser.close()
    if not parser.candidates:
        return _html_residual_extract(value)
    best = max(parser.candidates, key=lambda item: item["score"])
    return best["text"], {
        "candidate_nodes": len(parser.candidates),
        "best_score": round(best["score"], 2),
    }

def _html_jsonld_extract(value):
    matches = _html_re.findall(
        r'(?is)<script[^>]+type=["\']application/ld\+json["\'][^>]*>(.*?)</script>',
        value,
    )
    values = []
    parsed = 0
    for payload in matches:
        try:
            item = _html_json.loads(payload)
        except _html_json.JSONDecodeError:
            continue
        parsed += 1
        nodes = (
            item
            if isinstance(item, list)
            else item.get("@graph", [item])
            if isinstance(item, dict)
            else []
        )
        for node in nodes:
            if isinstance(node, dict):
                for key in (
                    "headline",
                    "name",
                    "description",
                    "articleBody",
                ):
                    item_value = node.get(key)
                    if isinstance(item_value, str):
                        values.append(item_value)
    return _html_normalize(" ".join(values)), {
        "jsonld_scripts": len(matches),
        "jsonld_parsed": parsed,
    }

def _html_load_or_cache(target_documents):
    HTML_EVAL_ROOT.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
    HTML_EVAL_IMPL_DIR.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
    records = []
    if HTML_EVAL_RAW_PATH.exists():
        with HTML_EVAL_RAW_PATH.open(encoding="utf-8") as handle:
            for line in handle:
                if line.strip():
                    records.append(_html_json.loads(line))
        if len(records) >= target_documents:
            return records[:target_documents], "cache"
    from datasets import load_dataset

    records = []
    skipped_oversized = 0
    stream = load_dataset(
        HTML_EVAL_DATASET,
        split=HTML_EVAL_SPLIT,
        streaming=True,
        revision=HTML_EVAL_REVISION,
    )
    with HTML_EVAL_RAW_PATH.open("w", encoding="utf-8") as handle:
        for source_index, source in enumerate(stream):
            html = source.get("html") or ""
            if not html or len(html) > _HTML_EVAL_MAX_CHARS:
                skipped_oversized += 1
                continue
            record = {
                "source_index": source_index,
                "c4_shard": source.get("c4_shard"),
                "timestamp": source.get("c4_timestamp"),
                "url": source.get("url"),
                "html": html,
                "reference_text": source.get("text") or "",
            }
            handle.write(
                _html_json.dumps(record, ensure_ascii=False) + "\n"
            )
            records.append(record)
            if len(records) >= target_documents:
                break
    HTML_EVAL_MANIFEST_PATH.write_text(
        _html_json.dumps(
            {
                "dataset": HTML_EVAL_DATASET,
                "revision": HTML_EVAL_REVISION,
                "split": HTML_EVAL_SPLIT,
                "selection": "first sequential non-empty HTML records under 500,000 characters",
                "requested_documents": target_documents,
                "retained_documents": len(records),
                "skipped_oversized_or_empty": skipped_oversized,
                "raw_path": str(HTML_EVAL_RAW_PATH),
            },
            ensure_ascii=False,
            indent=2,
        ),
        encoding="utf-8",
    )
    return records, "stream"

def run_html_technique_evaluation(target_documents):
    records, selection_source = _html_load_or_cache(target_documents)
    techniques = [

    aggregate = {

            document_metrics = {

    for library, available in _HTML_EVAL_LIBRARY_STATUS.items():

    result = {

_real_functions = r'''def _html_trafilatura_extract(value, url=None):
    extracted = _html_trafilatura.extract(
        value,
        url=url,
        include_comments=False,
        include_tables=True,
        deduplicate=False,
        output_format="txt",
    ) or ""
    return _html_normalize(extracted), {"library": "trafilatura"}

def _html_justext_extract(value):
    paragraphs = _html_justext.justext(
        value,
        _html_justext.get_stoplist("English"),
    )
    selected = [
        paragraph.text
        for paragraph in paragraphs
        if not paragraph.is_boilerplate and paragraph.text
    ]
    return "\n\n".join(selected), {
        "paragraphs": len(paragraphs),
        "content_paragraphs": len(selected),
    }

def _html_inscriptis_extract(value):
    return _html_inscriptis.get_text(value).strip(), {"library": "inscriptis"}

def _html_resiliparse_extract(value):
    extracted = _html_resiliparse_extract(
        value,
        preserve_formatting=True,
        main_content=True,
        comments=False,
    )
    return extracted.strip(), {"library": "resiliparse"}

def _html_readability_extract(value):
    summary_html = _HtmlReadabilityDocument(value).summary(
        html_partial=True
    )
    extracted, signals = _html_residual_extract(summary_html)
    return extracted, {"library": "readability-lxml", **signals}

def _html_collect_metadata_strings(value):
    values = []
    if isinstance(value, dict):
        for key, item in value.items():
            if key in {"headline", "name", "description", "articleBody"} and isinstance(item, str):
                values.append(item)
            else:
                values.extend(_html_collect_metadata_strings(item))
    elif isinstance(value, list):
        for item in value:
            values.extend(_html_collect_metadata_strings(item))
    return values

def _html_extruct_extract(value):
    extracted = _html_extruct.extract(value, syntaxes=["json-ld"])
    values = _html_collect_metadata_strings(extracted.get("json-ld", []))
    return _html_normalize(" ".join(values)), {
        "library": "extruct",
        "jsonld_records": len(extracted.get("json-ld", [])),
    }

'''
_techniques_old = '''    techniques = [
        (
            "residual_markup",
            "Residual markup removal",

            _html_residual_extract,

        ("jsonld_metadata", "Structured metadata extraction", "Transparent local JSON-LD control", _html_jsonld_extract, "metadata only"),
        ("trafilatura", "Trafilatura", "trafilatura 2.2.0", _html_trafilatura_extract, "library main-content extraction"),

        ("extruct", "extruct", "extruct 0.18.0", _html_extruct_extract, "library structured metadata extraction"),
    ]
'''

async with cm.get_context() as ctx:

import marimo._code_mode as cm
from html import escape

techniques = [
    {
        'key': 'trafilatura', 'title': 'Trafilatura — DOM main-content extraction',
        'family': 'Heuristic DOM extraction',
        'description': 'Parses the HTML tree, removes known non-content regions, and combines structural and text-density signals to retain article-like prose.',
        'steps': [('RAW HTML', 'URL + DOM'), ('PRUNE', 'navigation / ads'), ('SCORE', 'content candidates'), ('TEXT', 'article-like output')],
        'decision': 'Evaluate retained text against the supplied C4 text only as an agreement proxy; use human labels for extraction quality.'
    },
    {
        'key': 'justext', 'title': 'jusText — block-density boilerplate classification',
        'family': 'Heuristic block classification',
        'description': 'Splits an HTML page into text blocks and classifies them using text length, stopword density, link density, and neighboring-block context.',
        'steps': [('RAW HTML', 'page tree'), ('BLOCKS', 'paragraph candidates'), ('CLASSIFY', 'density + context'), ('TEXT', 'non-boilerplate blocks')],
        'decision': 'The executable run uses English stopwords because this auxiliary C4 corpus is English; this is not a Hindi threshold recommendation.'
    },
    {
        'key': 'inscriptis', 'title': 'Inscriptis — layout-aware HTML rendering',
        'family': 'Layout-preserving HTML to text',
        'description': 'Traverses HTML while retaining display-oriented boundaries for paragraphs, lists, and tables instead of concatenating all node text.',
        'steps': [('RAW HTML', 'markup + order'), ('TREE WALK', 'display semantics'), ('BOUNDARIES', 'lists / tables / blocks'), ('TEXT', 'layout-aware output')],
        'decision': 'Measure layout preservation separately from main-content precision: more retained text can include boilerplate.'
    },
    {
        'key': 'resiliparse', 'title': 'Resiliparse — high-throughput main-content text',
        'family': 'Scale-oriented DOM extraction',
        'description': 'Uses an optimized HTML parser and main-content-aware plain-text extraction path for source-artifact-first crawl processing.',
        'steps': [('RAW HTML', 'source record'), ('FAST PARSE', 'optimized DOM'), ('MAIN CONTENT', 'candidate filtering'), ('TEXT', 'high-throughput output')],
        'decision': 'Throughput is not a quality claim; compare retained content and failure cases by source domain before production use.'
    },
    {
        'key': 'readability', 'title': 'readability-lxml — semantic article scoring',
        'family': 'Readability-style DOM extraction',
        'description': 'Scores DOM containers for article-like density and semantics, selects the strongest candidate, then renders its remaining text.',
        'steps': [('RAW HTML', 'DOM nodes'), ('SCORE', 'density + semantics'), ('SELECT', 'best article node'), ('TEXT', 'candidate article')],
        'decision': 'Short documents, lists, and non-article pages are important false-deletion cases; inspect them separately rather than tuning by yield.'
    },
    {
        'key': 'extruct', 'title': 'extruct — structured metadata extraction',
        'family': 'Structured-data extraction',
        'description': 'Parses embedded JSON-LD and extracts structured fields such as headline, name, description, and article body where publishers supply them.',
        'steps': [('RAW HTML', 'embedded scripts'), ('JSON-LD', 'parse schema'), ('FIELDS', 'headline / body'), ('METADATA', 'routing + provenance')],
        'decision': 'Metadata extraction complements article extraction. Its character yield must not be compared directly with prose extractors.'
    },
]
colors = [('#0f766e', '#155e75'), ('#7c3aed', '#4338ca'), ('#b45309', '#9a3412'), ('#166534', '#065f46'), ('#1d4ed8', '#1e3a8a'), ('#be123c', '#881337')]

def svg_for(item, left, right):
    boxes = []
    for index, (heading, detail) in enumerate(item['steps']):
        x = 26 + index * 250
        boxes.append(
            f'<rect x="{x}" y="82" width="214" height="118" rx="18" fill="url(#g{index})" stroke="#e2e8f0" stroke-opacity=".35"/>'
            f'<text x="{x+107}" y="125" text-anchor="middle" fill="white" font-family="system-ui" font-size="18" font-weight="700">{escape(heading)}</text>'
            f'<text x="{x+107}" y="156" text-anchor="middle" fill="#dbeafe" font-family="system-ui" font-size="14">{escape(detail)}</text>'
        )
    arrows = ''.join(
        f'<path d="M{240 + index*250} 141 H{266 + index*250}" stroke="#bfdbfe" stroke-width="5" marker-end="url(#arrow)"/>'
        for index in range(3)
    )
    return f'''<svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 1026 232" role="img" aria-label="{escape(item['title'])} data flow">
  <defs>
    <linearGradient id="g0" x1="0" x2="1"><stop stop-color="{left}"/><stop offset="1" stop-color="{right}"/></linearGradient>
    <linearGradient id="g1" x1="0" x2="1"><stop stop-color="#334155"/><stop offset="1" stop-color="#1e293b"/></linearGradient>
    <linearGradient id="g2" x1="0" x2="1"><stop stop-color="#475569"/><stop offset="1" stop-color="#334155"/></linearGradient>
    <linearGradient id="g3" x1="0" x2="1"><stop stop-color="#0369a1"/><stop offset="1" stop-color="#075985"/></linearGradient>
    <marker id="arrow" markerWidth="10" markerHeight="10" refX="9" refY="3" orient="auto"><path d="M0,0 L0,6 L9,3 z" fill="#bfdbfe"/></marker>
  </defs>
  <rect width="1026" height="232" rx="24" fill="#0f172a"/>
  <circle cx="42" cy="37" r="9" fill="#38bdf8"/><text x="62" y="44" fill="#e2e8f0" font-family="system-ui" font-size="19" font-weight="700">{escape(item['family'])}</text>
  {''.join(boxes)}{arrows}
</svg>'''

async with cm.get_context() as ctx:
    anchor = next(cell for cell in ctx.cells if cell.name == 'html_eval_run').id
    existing = {cell.name: cell for cell in ctx.cells if cell.name}
    for item, (left, right) in zip(techniques, colors):
        svg = svg_for(item, left, right)
        explanation_name = f"{item['key']}_explanation"
        execution_name = f"{item['key']}_execution"
        explanation_code = f'''{explanation_name}_view = mo.vstack([\n    mo.md("""### {item['title']}\n**What it does.** {item['description']}\n\n**Evaluation boundary.** {item['decision']}"""),\n    mo.Html({svg!r}),\n])\n{explanation_name}_view'''
        execution_code = f'''{execution_name}_result = run_html_technique_sample("{item['key']}")\n{execution_name}_view = mo.vstack([\n    mo.md("#### Executable corpus run — {item['title']}\nRuns the installed library on the cached 30-document raw-HTML subset. The table exposes measurements only; it does not render source-page content."),\n    mo.ui.table([{execution_name}_result]),\n])\n{execution_name}_view'''
        for name, code, visible in ((explanation_name, explanation_code, False), (execution_name, execution_code, True)):
            cell = existing.get(name)
            if cell:
                ctx.edit_cell(cell.id, code=code, hide_code=visible)
                current_id = cell.id
            else:
                current_id = ctx.create_cell(code, after=anchor, name=name, hide_code=not visible)
            ctx.run_cell(current_id)
            anchor = current_id
    print('installed explanation → executable-run pairs for six real extractors')
